Male Infertility: There is always hope

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The stigma surrounding male infertility

Unique Selling Point:
When unable to conceive, many couples present themselves at fertility clinics for assessment and treatment. in 40 % of the cases, male infertility is the cause. This is not widely known.
Stigma often results in males not presenting themselves for assessment.
Male Infertility is a treatable condition.
We speak to couples where the men have been infertile and hear how they coped with the stigma, the treatment they had, and the coupe's joy in conceiving.
We also hear how some men fall out of male infertility treatment, because of the ongoing stigma, and the length it takes ...and marriages collapse.

Summary:
Why a program now on male infertility? According to Dr Thato Moata who expert in male infertility, male infertility is on the increase world wide. It's also been neglected in the past. Also Carte Blanche has never done a program on male infertility. Also there remains huge stigma surrounding male infertility. Stories we present on Carte Blanche can help reduce the stigma.

The context is in 40% of presenting couples at fertility clinics, the issues lie with the men. What are the common causes? 50% of these conditions can be reversed, according to Dr Moata. But he adds 80 to 90 per cent of all male fertility cases can be treated with modern medicine such as our one case study will tell us - Noleen Root's husband Antonie underwent 2 years of specialised hormonal treatment with Prof Kruger because he had zero sperm. The couple conceived twins.

The story can be set against SA's and Africa's first fertility show.


Further information:
Important case studies can be Elie Kuaiky a SA Lebanese born man who had azoospermia - no sperm, and the struggles he had dealing with the stigma - after treatment he and his wife were able to have twins - huge joy - now he councils couples. We can also feature a speaker at the conference Molatelo Mainetje-Bossman who has spoken out about her infertility through her documentary film When Babies Don’t Come where she documents her 10-year struggle with infertility. Through the film, Mainetje-Bossman has not only inspired many people but has also given a voice to many men and women with the same condition. She can add that you never hear of men in some communities who are infertile, so taboo it is.
We do bring in Prof Kruger who successfully treated Noleen and Antonie Roots and he can fill us in on advanced treatments for male infertility. He received much acclaim when he found out that male infertility can be diagnosed by the look of sperm. When a man changes his life style for example, and stops smoking which has lead to the infertility, or stops taking steroids, the "look" of the sperm change - often an indication that the man is fertile again. He and a software engineer designed a software program which scans graphics of sperm and make diagnostical assessments of the sperm.

Press Release:


Treating Male Infertility
It’s something rarely spoken of and one of society’s longstanding taboos – men who struggle with infertility. Studies show that in over 40 percent of couples attending fertility clinics in South Africa, male infertility lies at the heart of the problem. Abnormal sperm production as a result of medical conditions that can often be reversed – like obesity or drug use – have led experts to agree that with the right intervention, male infertility can be treated. So why are some men so reluctant to seek help?
Producer: Michael Duffet | Presenter: Claire Mawisa | Research: Sinethemba Nogude


Script:


CARTE BLANCHE – MALE INFERTILITY

script


Elie Kouaiky: The day I was told I couldn't have kids in my face that day I'll never forget because I arrived home and parked the car and started crying.

VO
For most people, having a child is one of the most important events of their lives but .being unable to conceive can be life-changing….

Link:
All too often fertility is seen as a woman's issue. But in 42 percent of the couples who attend fertility clinics in south Africa it's actually the men who are infertile.

V/O: [New B-roll on beach]
In 2007, Elie Kouaiky went through exhaustive tests after months of trying to conceive with his partner Amanda. The diagnosis? azoospermia – where the semen contains no sperm. He was devastated.

Elie:
It's lonely. It's dark. You feel worthless. …..i felt small

V/O: {13 sec}
Antonie Roets was diagnosed with brain cancer in 2002… His pituitary gland had to be removed, and, as a result, his system could no longer produce sperm naturally. Nine years later he met Nadine, and they fell in love.

Antonie:
Both of us had children from previous marriages. And because we were committed to the relationship we thought that having our own children will solidify the bond.

V/O:
For both men, a diagnosis of azoospermia seemed to put an end to their dreams, but they were not alone. I in 6 couples in south Africa can’t conceive


V/O: {7 sec}
In March this year, the first Fertility Show in Africa was held in Johannesburg, One of the organisers, Saskia Williams heads up the Infertility Awareness Association of South Africa – an organisation that aims to break the silence surrounding infertility.

Saskia:
People still feel ashamed of having it. Especially males. They don't speak as much as women as women we are more open We want to find support. Men find it very hard to talk about A show like this shows them that they're not alone.

V/O: {15 sec}
According to gynaecologist Doctor Thato Maoto the causes for male infertility vary from environmental, hormonal, disease, physiological and lifestyle factors such as obesity, smoking and substance abuse. He says in most cases there is a medical solution…

Moato:
About 50 percent of patients who come to us with an identifiable cause of male infertility, there is a reversible cause. But even more than that even in the other 50 percent where we don't find a reversible cause there's still treatment options that we can do.



V/O: {16 sec}
As the Roets were to discover, Despite his diagnosis, Antonie and Noleen were not ready to give up on having their own children. In 2012 they consulted with fertility expert, Professor Thinus Kruger. He and his team were responsible for South Africa's first test tube baby, in 1985.

Dr Kruger:
In his case, I realised that the pituitary gland was damaged if there's damage of pituitary gland then there's no function of the testes, but luckily we had a solution and that is to give him the correct hormones to reintroduce sperm production.

V/O: {6 sec}
After six months of hormonal treatment, Antonie’s system started to produce sperm. Noelene also had to undergo treatment.

Noelene:
So I would also have to go onto fertility treatments and injections daily and things like that so it was a whole regime on my side.

V/O: {11 sec}
Noelene’s eggs were fertilised with Antonie’s sperm in a process called intracytoplasmic sperm injection. Successfully fertilised embryos were implanted into Noelene’s uterus. Then came days of waiting and testing.

Noelene:
We got the SMS just before 12:00 that night to say that it was unsuccessful. And we just literally burst into tears. The sister who was on duty rang us and said she was sorry, but they must not give up…. She gave us a pep talk……this was at midnight.

V/O: {4 sec}
At this stage, according to Professor Kruger, many couples abandon fertility treatment.

Prof K.
the world literature researched that very well and they say in spite of certain patients with good financial means, will still, due to emotional reasons, stop.

V/O: {10 sec}
Despite the challenges , the Roots were determined to press ahead and after six months they started the process all over again. Eighteen months later , Noelene finally fell pregnant with twins.

Claire
How does that feel, after years of trying injections, money, moods, stress, tears.

Antonie
It’s big, its big.

Prof Kruger:
I think the nurses were I remember that morning over the moon when they've heard the results and of course I felt the same – excited, happy. But it's again a journey so the pregnancy is what we want but now it's an ongoing journey to go to seven weeks and twelve weeks and hope that everything is still OK.

V/O: {10 sec}
And 28 months after starting fertility treatment, Hunter and Ava were born. But not every man finds it easy to accept that they are infertile when they are first diagnosed.


Dr Maoto
The first step is always acceptance. So, we usually recommend them seeing psychologists after the diagnosis because it can be devastating for the couple and for their relationship.

VO

Dr Maoto tells his patients that there are a number of medical treatments available – such as hormones, medicines, surgical procedures and a change in life style which will increase sperm count.. Yet despite this, some men fall out of treatment because of stigma.

Dr Moata:
Culturally unacceptable. So, it's difficult to be taking treatment weekly or daily and having to explain yourself when socially already you don't want the world to know that you're struggling with fertility.

VO
And social stigma is common to many other cultures – including Elie’s country of birth, Lebanon.

Elie:
In Lebanon it's a very taboo subject so men don't talk to each other about fertility and especially women do not talk to men about infertility.


rV/O: {3 sec}
After his diagnosis, Elie and Amanda had some difficult decisions to make.

Amanda
The option then is donor sperm or adoption, let’s talk about that. And so, our discussions behind closed doors were that we just could not agree.

V/O: {5 sec}
Then on holiday in Lebanon in 2009, Elie was persuaded to see another fertility doctor who advised him that he should undergo hormonal treatment.

Claire
So, the doctor gave you hope that you could produce sperm. What did that feel like?

Elie:
When I walked out of the elevator I was broken, like literally I was broken. I was crying. I was feeling weak. I felt vulnerable, very vulnerable.

V/O: {9 sec}
... And that's because he had been on this journey before. But Elie and his wife, Amanda, persevered with the treatment. This time, the doctor phoned with different news.

Elie:
‘Congratulations Mr Kouaiky, you are a dad.’ I never forget that. I was crying for three hours in the car. I stopped on the side of the road. I couldn't answer.

For Elie, going from infertility to now being a father of two vibrant TWINS is a testament to the advances that have been made in the treatment of male infertility. And Nolene’s advise for men who are infertile?

Nolene

Forget about the stigma. If you want kids etc etd











PROMOS

• In 42% of couples who undergo fertility treatment --- it’s the men who are found to be infertile. But experts say that the condition is almost always reversible.
• One in six couples in South Africa, who are actively trying to conceive, are infertile. experts say in 42% of couples who attend fertility clinics, it’s the men who have the problem.
• Fear and stigma --- two reasons why some men never seek help when trying to conceive. But experts say that in 42% of cases, male infertility is at the heart of the problem.

metadata.Summary: Why a program now on male infertility? According to Dr Thato Moata who expert in male infertility, male infertility is on the increase world wide. It's also been neglected in the past. Also Carte Blanche has never done a program on male infertility. Also there remains huge stigma surrounding male infertility. Stories we present on Carte Blanche can help reduce the stigma. The context is in 40% of presenting couples at fertility clinics, the issues lie with the men. What are the common causes? 50% of these conditions can be reversed, according to Dr Moata. But he adds 80 to 90 per cent of all male fertility cases can be treated with modern medicine such as our one case study will tell us - Noleen Root's husband Antonie underwent 2 years of specialised hormonal treatment with Prof Kruger because he had zero sperm. The couple conceived twins. The story can be set against SA's and Africa's first fertility show.
metadata.Further information: Important case studies can be Elie Kuaiky a SA Lebanese born man who had azoospermia - no sperm, and the struggles he had dealing with the stigma - after treatment he and his wife were able to have twins - huge joy - now he councils couples. We can also feature a speaker at the conference Molatelo Mainetje-Bossman who has spoken out about her infertility through her documentary film When Babies Don’t Come where she documents her 10-year struggle with infertility. Through the film, Mainetje-Bossman has not only inspired many people but has also given a voice to many men and women with the same condition. She can add that you never hear of men in some communities who are infertile, so taboo it is. We do bring in Prof Kruger who successfully treated Noleen and Antonie Roots and he can fill us in on advanced treatments for male infertility. He received much acclaim when he found out that male infertility can be diagnosed by the look of sperm. When a man changes his life style for example, and stops smoking which has lead to the infertility, or stops taking steroids, the "look" of the sperm change - often an indication that the man is fertile again. He and a software engineer designed a software program which scans graphics of sperm and make diagnostical assessments of the sperm.
